clue.text: Stop watching TV that shocks the kids

parts.note: to jack in is British slang for to give up or quit
the box is informal British slang for the television

explanation.surface: A warning that giving up television is upsetting the children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop watching TV' reads as one idiom: to jack in (quit) the box (the telly). 'watching' only links the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The toy is a lidded case from which a sprung clown leaps out, startling small children.

clue.text: Evergreen youth takes exercise for nothing

indicators.note: takes signals the youth taking in a new piece
for marks the swap, the exercise in place of the zero

parts.note: a junior is a young person
O looks like zero, nothing
PE is physical education, exercise at school

explanation.surface: A green young person exercises rather than idling.
explanation.walkthrough: PE (exercise) replaces O (nothing) in JUNIOR.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a coniferous shrub that keeps its needles all year, its berries flavouring gin.

clue.text: Maybe 21/50 cheap suit trousers fray, but not always

indicators.note: trousers as a verb means pockets or takes in, so the cheap suit holds the cut-down fray

parts.note: common means vulgar or cheap
a lawsuit is a legal action

indicators.note: but not removes the old word for always from the word before it

parts.note: ay, or aye, is an old word for always

explanation.surface: A shabby suit whose trousers only sometimes fray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' is a verb: COMMON ACTION (cheap suit) takes in FR, which is FRAY without AY (always).
explanation.definitionFit: 21/50 is a ratio of whole numbers written with numerator over denominator, as opposed to a decimal.

clue.text: Try quitting business that's banked in Asia

indicators.note: quitting means the three letters leave the longer word

parts.note: industry is business or commerce

explanation.surface: Giving up a firm that keeps its money in an Asian bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banked' suggests money, but it means having banks: a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river of Pakistan has banks along its course, so it is a watercourse in Asia.

clue.text: Ironically cutting successive balls through the slips?

definitions.meaning: a remark that cuts both ways is sharp on either side, like irony
in cricket, a batter who edges two balls in a row past the slip fielders has done it twice

explanation.surface: A sarcastic remark about consecutive deliveries snicked past the fielders.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the slips are fielders beside the wicketkeeper, and an edge is a ball glancing off the bat's side.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-sided blade cuts both ways, as an ironic comment can backfire; and in cricket two edges in a row.

clue.text: Get upset about unknown people no longer with us

indicators.note: about means going around the unknown letter
upset, in a down clue, turns the word upside down so it reads backwards

parts.note: to get something is to see it, understand
X is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Becoming distressed thinking about strangers who have died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no longer with us' suggests the dead, but means former partners.
explanation.definitionFit: Former spouses or partners are no longer in a relationship with the speaker.

clue.text: A cold wet nursery deters boy playing

indicators.note: playing means fooling about, so the letters move around

explanation.surface: A chilly, damp crèche that puts a child off playing there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nursery' looks like a place for children; it is where young shellfish are raised.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellfish are farmed on these seabed patches, a chilly underwater nursery for molluscs.

clue.text: To transfer extra, initially this restriction must be accepted

definitions.text: To transfer extra, initially this restriction must be accepted

parts.note: to second someone is to transfer them to another post

indicators.note: must be accepted means the word for extra takes the pieces inside it

parts.note: more means extra

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word this

parts.note: a gag is a restriction on speech

explanation.surface: Taking out more money on a home means agreeing to another charge on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must be accepted' signals insertion and 'initially' takes a first letter; read whole, the clue also describes the loan itself, a further charge the borrower must accept.
explanation.definitionFit: A further loan secured on the same property moves extra borrowing onto it, with a lien the lender insists upon.

clue.text: A black suit is useful kit for a burial

definitions.meaning: one of the two black suits in a deck of cards
digging tools, needed to dig a grave

explanation.surface: A mourner's dark suit, practical clothing for a funeral.
explanation.definitionFit: The card suit of black leaves, and the digging tools used to open a grave.

clue.text: Like Bill, Ben, Tom, Dick, Harry and me?

indicators.note: to harry is to harass or worry, so the letters that follow are knocked about into a new order

explanation.surface: A list of everyday men's names, with the setter tacking themself on at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like the last name in the list, as in 'Tom, Dick and Harry', but it is the anagram signal working on AND ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill, Ben, Tom and Dick are all given names, so each one is a label borne by people who carry that title.

clue.text: Lee proves getting sacked is a bad way to avoid the early commute

definitions.text: a bad way to avoid the early commute

indicators.note: being sacked throws things into disorder, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Lee demonstrates that losing a job is a poor way to dodge the rush-hour journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting sacked' is the anagram signal on LEE PROVES; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying asleep past the alarm does mean missing the morning journey to work, though hardly in a good way.

clue.text: Camp on bank next to the water

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another comes after it

parts.note: a bank or kitty of shared money is a pool
a camp is a faction or party, a side in a dispute

explanation.surface: Pitching a tent on a riverbank by the water's edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' tempts as a river bank, but it is the money sense, a pool.
explanation.definitionFit: The area at the edge of a swimming bath is where loungers sit beside the water.

clue.text: More than 500 following pop diva out of church

indicators.note: following places the numeral after the trimmed name
taken out of says the church letters leave the singer's name

parts.note: Beyonce is the American pop superstar
CE is the Church of England
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: Over 500 fans trail a pop star as she leaves a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' signals the removal, leaving BEYON, and 'following' puts the numeral last; 'church' is a crossword regular for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: As a preposition it means past or exceeding, as in 'over and above'.

clue.text: Grass skirts either sex modelled differently

indicators.note: skirts means goes around the edges of, so the grass wraps the other piece

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass
either sex is F or M, written out as F OR M

explanation.surface: A grass skirt worn by men or women, cut to a new pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirts' signals wrapping. 'either sex' is read literally as two letters joined by 'or', the trick that makes the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaped anew or made over in a changed pattern; a remodelled thing has been given fresh shape.

clue.text: Barrage of questions Sally let go, keeping quiet

indicators.note: keeping means the attack holds the quiet letter inside

parts.note: a sally is a sudden attack, a raid
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
to fire someone is to let them go from a job

explanation.surface: Sally was dismissed because of a barrage of questions she didn't answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sally' is not a woman but a sortie, RAID, which keeps P inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes questions put in quick succession, like shots from a gun.

clue.text: A book that is unfinished doesn't come to an end

indicators.note: unfinished means the Latin phrase loses its final letter

parts.note: id est is the Latin phrase for 'that is', abbreviated i.e.

explanation.surface: A book left half written never reaches its conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that is' is the Latin ID EST; 'unfinished' drops its last letter T to give IDES.
explanation.definitionFit: To last or endure is to carry on without stopping, as in 'the memory remains'.

clue.text: Old German in my French group only good at Spanish?

indicators.note: in places the old German letters inside the French-plus-group pair

parts.note: mon is French for my
a lot is a group or batch

explanation.surface: An elderly German in a French group speaks only Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: '?' marks the definition as an example: someone speaking only Spanish knows one language.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who speaks a single language is limited to one tongue, Spanish here.

clue.text: Periodic problem, stuff I forgot to mention

parts.note: to cram is to stuff tightly
PS, a postscript, adds what the writer forgot to say

explanation.surface: Someone muttering about a nuisance and all the bits they left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodic' means menstrual here, the painful spasms of a period.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscle spasms come with menstruation, so they are a monthly complaint for many women.

clue.text: Go out back visiting my mate in the outback

indicators.note: visiting means the reversed word stays inside the exclamation

parts.note: cor is an exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

indicators.note: back means the word for go out is read backwards

parts.note: the tide going out is the ebb

explanation.surface: Leave by the back to call on my friend in the Australian bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' is the exclamation COR, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: It is Australian slang for a friend or pal, used in the bush.

clue.text: Craft is likely to run on air

indicators.note: on air means broadcast, spoken out, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: something that is likely to run or function 'would work'

explanation.surface: A boat or aircraft that will probably run on air power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' looks like a vessel but is a skill; 'would work', spoken, gives the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpentry and making things from timber is a manual skill or trade.

clue.text: Like wearing boots? That's great

indicators.note: wearing means being inside the footwear

parts.note: kicks is slang for shoes or boots
as means like

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled at the idea of putting on boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' signals insertion; 'kicks' for footwear is American slang. 'That's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: It is American slang for something excellent or terrific.

clue.text: Happen to be coming in or going out?

parts.note: the sea's tide is always either coming in or going out

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether someone is arriving or leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful description of the tide.
explanation.definitionFit: The old verb means befall, as in 'woe befall you', so it means to occur to someone.

clue.text: Highly principled old lady ambushed by cur and jerk

indicators.note: ambushed by puts the mother between the two attackers

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
a tic is an involuntary jerk
one's old lady is one's mother, MA

explanation.surface: A strait-laced elderly woman set upon by a mongrel and an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jerk' tempts as a fool, but here it is a twitch; 'and' links DOG and TIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone rigidly principled holds fixed opinions and insists on them as unarguable.

clue.text: Trouble in Scotland for one idiot heading north

indicators.note: heading north, in a down clue, reads the letters upwards

parts.note: eg is exempli gratia, for example or for one
dim means stupid, like an idiot

explanation.surface: A troublesome fool travelling north into Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'idiot' gives DIM, an adjective; fair because it stands for idiotic.
explanation.definitionFit: These tiny biting flies plague Highland summers in swarms.

clue.text: Uniquely large rear end of pop diva

indicators.note: a large rear end of the name keeps its back four letters, dropping the start

parts.note: Beyonce is the American pop superstar

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark about a pop star's famously big bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'large rear end' is the longer tail of BEYONCE, all but its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: It means on one occasion only, a single time, hence uniquely.

clue.text: Painful method usually employed to break off toenail

indicators.note: to break means to split the jumbled letters open and sit inside them
off means gone bad or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: MO is modus operandi, a person's usual method

explanation.surface: A sore, tried-and-tested technique for ripping away a toenail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' signals the anagram, ETIONAL, and 'to break' puts modus operandi's abbreviation inside, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A painful scene in the figurative sense is one full of feeling and upsetting.

clue.text: Play first shot?

parts.note: a shot of spirits is a dram
A is a grade meaning first or top

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to take the opening shot in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' gives A, as in an A grade or A1.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage play or theatrical work for actors is a piece of theatre.

clue.text: Still sorting out three sevens divided by fifty?

indicators.note: divided by means the jumbled letters are split by the numeral placed among them
sorting out rearranges the letters of the two words

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A sum: twenty-one shared among fifty, as an arithmetic puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divided by' looks like arithmetic, but L (fifty) is put inside the anagram of THREE SEVENS.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb it means all the same or even so, like 'however'.
